patient.chief_complaint: Found unresponsive at home with serum sodium 110 mEq/L (profound hyponatremia), confusion, and on day 6 developed bilateral lower limb weakness and areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 64-year-old woman found unresponsive at home by her neighbor. She reported mild malaise, decreased appetite, and mild stomach discomfort the day prior. On emergency evaluation, she was obtunded (GCS 9) with confused speech. Laboratory studies revealed profound hyponatremia with serum sodium 110 mEq/L — markedly below her last documented value of 136 mEq/L three months prior on the same medication regimen. Serum osmolality was 235 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality 413 mOsm/kg with high urine sodium consistent with SIADH. CT head and neck were normal. MRI brain showed multiple nonspecific T2 hyperintensities without osmotic demyelination. EEG showed mild diffuse slowing — no epileptiform discharges. CSF on day 1 showed protein 52 mg/dL with 1 WBC. Initial management focused on SIADH treatment with hydrochlorothiazide discontinuation, hypertonic saline, and IV antibiotics (empiric). Sodium was corrected from 110 to 120 mEq/L over 24 hours — within safe range (10 mEq/L/24h). By hospital day 5 she was improving cognitively and transferred to the ward. However, on day 6 she complained of new lower back pain followed by bilateral leg numbness and tingling and gait instability. Neurological examination then revealed bilateral lower limb weakness and areflexia — findings not present at admission. The motor and sensory findings emerged on day 6, after correction of the hyponatremia, having been preceded at presentation by the dominant hyponatremic encephalopathy.

cardiac_monitoring.impression: Continuous inpatient telemetry through the period of maximal weakness. Autonomic involvement affects about two thirds of patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome and is a leading cause of in-hospital death, so this recording is a monitoring requirement rather than a diagnostic test: what it looks for is the bradyarrhythmia, the pause beyond 3 seconds and the blood-pressure lability that trigger ICU escalation, alongside serial respiratory function. Beyond the rate, the recording is normal. That is the expected result in this patient and it is not a wasted test: the value of monitoring in this disease lies in what it excludes during the window in which dysautonomia can appear.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP, presenting with severe SIADH-related hyponatraemia and delayed motor signs

differential.diagnosis: Primary SIADH from CNS / pulmonary / drug cause with secondary encephalopathy
differential.key_features: Profound hyponatremia (Na 110) explains encephalopathy; need to identify primary aetiology (here, GBS-associated SIADH); motor signs emerging on day 6 redirect to a primary neurological cause.
Encephalopathy and seizures possible; CSF cell count and autoimmune encephalitis panel cover; albuminocytologic dissociation favors GBS.
Risk if sodium corrected too quickly; MRI brain shows characteristic pontine lesion; presentation typically delayed 2–6 days.
Liver function unsupportive; ammonia not consistent.
Bilateral symmetric motor signs and areflexia not consistent with focal vascular event; MRI excludes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Start continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry for the period of maximal weakness and keep it running alongside serial respiratory function. Autonomic instability affects about two thirds of patients and is a leading cause of in-hospital death: bradyarrhythmias, pauses beyond 3 seconds and blood-pressure lability are what trigger ICU escalation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm at 92 bpm throughout with no bradyarrhythmia, pause or AV block — a normal recording, which is the expected result and excludes the dysautonomia that would escalate care during the window in which it can appear

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Cautious sodium correction (≤10 mEq/L per 24 h, ideally 6–8 mEq/L) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Workup SIADH cause — GBS itself is recognised as causing SIADH; identify other contributors (drugs, lung, CNS).
Initiate IVIG / plasma exchange once GBS is supported by EMG and CSF.
MRI brain to exclude central pontine myelinolysis after sodium correction.
contraindicated_actions: Do not over-correct sodium (>12 mEq/L per 24 h) — osmotic demyelination risk.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
key_reasoning_points: GBS is a recognised cause of SIADH; profound hyponatraemia can dominate the presenting picture and delay diagnosis.
Encephalopathy in hyponatraemia must be distinguished from primary autoimmune encephalitis or osmotic demyelination.
Slow sodium correction protects against central pontine myelinolysis, particularly important once GBS treatment is underway.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the entire syndrome to hyponatraemia and miss the underlying GBS once motor signs emerge.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS-associated SIADH can produce profound hyponatremia; the appearance of areflexia and ascending weakness after correction unmasks the primary neurological diagnosis.
